cards.title: What is the supreme law of the land?
cards.body: The Constitution is the oldest still-functioning written national constitution in the world.
cards.prompt: What is the supreme law of the land?
cards.context: Every other law -- federal, state, or local -- must yield to it under the Supremacy Clause (Article VI).

cards.title: What does the Constitution do?
cards.body: It is famously short -- about 4,400 words in its original form, the shortest of any major world government's founding charter.
cards.prompt: What does the Constitution do?
cards.context: It creates the three branches, divides power between federal and state government, and lists what the government cannot do to its citizens.

cards.title: The idea of self-government is in the first three words of the Constitution. What are these words?
cards.body: Those three words are written in the original document at roughly triple the size of the rest of the text.
cards.prompt: The idea of self-government is in the first three words of the Constitution. What are these words?
cards.context: The framers opened with the source of the government's authority, not the government itself -- power flows up from citizens, not down from a ruler.

cards.title: What is an amendment?
cards.body: Thousands of amendments have been proposed in Congress; only 27 have ever been ratified.
cards.prompt: What is an amendment?
cards.context: The framers built in a deliberately difficult process (Article V) so the Constitution could evolve without being easy to hijack.

cards.title: What do we call the first ten amendments to the Constitution?
cards.body: James Madison, who once argued a bill of rights was unnecessary, ended up writing it.
cards.prompt: What do we call the first ten amendments to the Constitution?
cards.context: States only agreed to ratify the Constitution after being promised an explicit list of protected rights -- this was that promise, kept.

cards.title: What is one right or freedom from the First Amendment?
cards.body: It's called the 'First' Amendment by position, not importance -- the framers didn't rank the Bill of Rights.
cards.prompt: What is one right or freedom from the First Amendment?
cards.context: The First Amendment bundles five distinct freedoms into 45 words, all aimed at keeping the government out of how people think, worship, and speak.

cards.title: How many amendments does the Constitution have?
cards.body: The most recent, the 27th, took 202 years to ratify -- proposed in 1789, finally adopted in 1992.
cards.prompt: How many amendments does the Constitution have?
cards.context: 27 in 235+ years is a slow pace by design -- ratification needs three-fourths of the states to agree.

cards.title: What did the Declaration of Independence do?
cards.body: It didn't take effect until the Continental Congress actually voted for independence on July 2, 1776 -- the 4th is when the text was adopted.
cards.prompt: What did the Declaration of Independence do?
cards.context: It wasn't a legal document that created a government -- it was a public justification for a rebellion already underway.
answers: said that the United States is free (from Great Britain)

cards.title: What are two rights in the Declaration of Independence?
cards.body: The phrase has no legal force in U.S. law -- the Declaration is a statement of principle, not a binding statute.
cards.prompt: What are two rights in the Declaration of Independence?
cards.context: Jefferson borrowed the framework from Locke's 'life, liberty, and property' but swapped in 'pursuit of happiness.'

cards.title: What is freedom of religion?
cards.body: Several of the original colonies had official state religions even after independence -- Massachusetts didn't disestablish its state church until 1833.
cards.prompt: What is freedom of religion?
cards.context: The First Amendment protects belief AND disbelief equally -- the government can neither establish a religion nor punish someone for lacking one.
answers: You can practice any religion, or not practice a religion.

cards.title: What is the economic system in the United States?
cards.body: The Constitution itself is largely silent on economic system -- it grants Congress commerce powers but doesn't mandate capitalism by name.
cards.prompt: What is the economic system in the United States?
cards.context: Private ownership and market pricing drive most production and trade decisions, with government regulation layered on top rather than replacing it.

cards.title: What is the 'rule of law'?
cards.body: United States v. Nixon (1974) is the clearest modern test of this principle -- the Supreme Court ordered a sitting president to comply with a subpoena.
cards.prompt: What is the 'rule of law'?
cards.context: It's the idea that binds a president to the same courts as any citizen -- power comes with legal limits, not around them.
answers: No one is above the law.

cards.title: Name one branch or part of the government.
cards.body: The Constitution describes the branches in that order -- Congress in Article I, the President in Article II, the courts in Article III.
cards.prompt: Name one branch or part of the government.
cards.context: Three branches, each given a distinct job: Congress writes laws, the President enforces them, the courts interpret them.

cards.title: What stops one branch of government from becoming too powerful?
cards.body: Montesquieu's writing on separated powers directly influenced the framers, especially Madison.
cards.prompt: What stops one branch of government from becoming too powerful?
cards.context: Each branch has a tool to restrain the others -- vetoes, overrides, confirmations, judicial review -- so no single branch can act alone indefinitely.

cards.title: Who is in charge of the executive branch?
cards.body: The executive branch also includes 15 Cabinet departments and millions of federal employees the President oversees only indirectly.
cards.prompt: Who is in charge of the executive branch?
cards.context: The President enforces and administers federal law, commands the military, and runs the executive agencies.

cards.title: Who makes federal laws?
cards.body: Only a small fraction of bills introduced in a given Congress -- typically under 5% -- ever become law.
cards.prompt: Who makes federal laws?
cards.context: A bill must pass both chambers in identical form and get the President's signature (or a veto override) to become law.

cards.title: What are the two parts of the U.S. Congress?
cards.body: The compromise nearly broke the Constitutional Convention before it was adopted.
cards.prompt: What are the two parts of the U.S. Congress?
cards.context: This split was the Great Compromise of 1787 -- the Senate gives every state equal footing, the House represents population.

cards.title: How many U.S. Senators are there?
cards.body: The Senate has had 100 members only since 1959, when Alaska and Hawaii became the 49th and 50th states.
cards.prompt: How many U.S. Senators are there?
cards.context: Two per state, regardless of population -- California and Wyoming get the same two votes in the Senate.

cards.title: We elect a U.S. Senator for how many years?
cards.body: Senators were originally chosen by state legislatures, not voters directly, until the 17th Amendment in 1913.
cards.prompt: We elect a U.S. Senator for how many years?
cards.context: Senate terms are staggered so only about a third of seats are up in any given election, giving the chamber more continuity than the House.

cards.title: Who is one of your state's U.S. Senators now?
cards.body: Every state gets exactly two, regardless of population -- the only chamber built that way.
cards.prompt: Who is one of your state's U.S. Senators now?
cards.context: This answer depends on where you live -- the USCIS test expects you to know your own current senators.

cards.title: The House of Representatives has how many voting members?
cards.body: In 1789 there were only 65 House members; the number grew with the country until Congress capped it.
cards.prompt: The House of Representatives has how many voting members?
cards.context: That number has been fixed by federal law since 1929 -- as population grows, each representative simply represents more people.

cards.title: We elect a U.S. Representative for how many years?
cards.body: All 435 House seats are up for election every single cycle, unlike the staggered Senate.
cards.prompt: We elect a U.S. Representative for how many years?
cards.context: The short term was intentional -- the House was designed to be the branch most directly and frequently accountable to voters.

cards.title: Name your U.S. Representative.
cards.body: Congressional districts are redrawn after each decennial census to keep them roughly equal in population.
cards.prompt: Name your U.S. Representative.
cards.context: This depends on your congressional district, redrawn roughly every ten years after the census.

cards.title: Who does a U.S. Senator represent?
cards.body: This statewide constituency is part of why Senate races often draw more national attention than individual House races.
cards.prompt: Who does a U.S. Senator represent?
cards.context: Unlike a House member tied to one district, a Senator's constituency is the entire state.

cards.title: Why do some states have more Representatives than other states?
cards.body: California currently has 52 House seats; several small states have only one.
cards.prompt: Why do some states have more Representatives than other states?
cards.context: House seats are apportioned by population after every census -- more residents means more seats, up to the 435 cap.

cards.title: We elect a President for how many years?
cards.body: The 22nd Amendment (1951) later capped a President at two elected terms, a limit that didn't exist for the first 150+ years.
cards.prompt: We elect a President for how many years?
cards.context: A four-year term balances stability against accountability -- long enough to govern, short enough to face voters again soon.

cards.title: In what month do we vote for President?
cards.body: November was chosen partly because harvests were in and winter travel hadn't yet made roads impassable.
cards.prompt: In what month do we vote for President?
cards.context: Congress set a uniform national Election Day in 1845 -- the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November.

cards.title: What is the name of the President of the United States now?
cards.body: The President is not elected by direct popular vote but by the Electoral College.
cards.prompt: What is the name of the President of the United States now?
cards.context: This answer changes with each election -- the USCIS test expects the sitting President at time of interview.

cards.title: What is the name of the Vice President of the United States now?
cards.body: John Adams, the first VP, called it 'the most insignificant office that ever the invention of man contrived.'
cards.prompt: What is the name of the Vice President of the United States now?
cards.context: The Vice President's main constitutional jobs are succession and breaking Senate ties -- everything else is by presidential assignment.

cards.title: If the President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
cards.body: Nine Vice Presidents have become President through the death or resignation of a sitting President.
cards.prompt: If the President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
cards.context: This line of succession is set by the Constitution and reinforced by the 25th Amendment's procedures.

cards.title: If both the President and the Vice President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
cards.body: No Speaker of the House has ever actually had to assume the presidency.
cards.prompt: If both the President and the Vice President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
cards.context: The Presidential Succession Act of 1947 set this order after the Vice Presidency, ahead of the Senate President pro tempore and Cabinet.

cards.title: Who is the Commander in Chief of the military?
cards.body: Congress, not the President, holds the constitutional power to formally declare war -- a split that's caused friction for over a century.
cards.prompt: Who is the Commander in Chief of the military?
cards.context: This puts the military under civilian control -- an elected official, not a general, holds ultimate authority.

cards.title: Who signs bills to become laws?
cards.body: If Congress adjourns during that 10-day window and the President doesn't sign, the bill dies -- a 'pocket veto.'
cards.prompt: Who signs bills to become laws?
cards.context: A bill passed by both chambers of Congress becomes law once the President signs it -- or becomes law automatically after 10 days if left unsigned.

cards.title: Who vetoes bills?
cards.body: Overrides are rare -- fewer than 10% of vetoes in U.S. history have been overridden.
cards.prompt: Who vetoes bills?
cards.context: A veto sends the bill back to Congress, which can override it with a two-thirds vote in both chambers.

cards.title: What does the President's Cabinet do?
cards.body: George Washington's original Cabinet had just four members: State, Treasury, War, and the Attorney General.
cards.prompt: What does the President's Cabinet do?
cards.context: The Cabinet has no constitutional power of its own -- it exists entirely to inform and advise the President's decisions.

cards.title: What are two Cabinet-level positions?
cards.body: There are 15 executive departments today, up from Washington's original four.
cards.prompt: What are two Cabinet-level positions?
cards.context: Each Secretary leads a federal department and sits in the presidential line of succession.

cards.title: What does the judicial branch do?
cards.body: The power of judicial review isn't explicitly written in the Constitution -- the Supreme Court claimed it itself in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
cards.prompt: What does the judicial branch do?
cards.context: Courts don't write or enforce law -- they interpret it, and can strike down laws that violate the Constitution.
answers: decides if a law goes against the Constitution

cards.title: What is the highest court in the United States?
cards.body: The Supreme Court didn't get its own building until 1935; before that it met inside the Capitol.
cards.prompt: What is the highest court in the United States?
cards.context: It's the final word on federal law and constitutional interpretation -- there's no appeal above it.

cards.title: How many justices are on the Supreme Court?
cards.body: The Court has had as few as five and as many as ten justices; it's been nine since 1869.
cards.prompt: How many justices are on the Supreme Court?
cards.context: The number isn't fixed by the Constitution -- Congress sets it by statute, and it's changed several times in history.

cards.title: Who is the Chief Justice of the United States now?
cards.body: Roberts was confirmed in 2005 at age 50, making him one of the youngest Chief Justices in modern history.
cards.prompt: Who is the Chief Justice of the United States now?
cards.context: The Chief Justice presides over the Court, assigns opinion-writing when in the majority, and presides over presidential impeachment trials in the Senate.

cards.title: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the federal government. What is one power of the federal government?
cards.body: States are explicitly forbidden from printing their own money or making treaties -- those powers are federal only.
cards.prompt: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the federal government. What is one power of the federal government?
cards.context: These are 'enumerated powers' -- specifically listed in Article I, Section 8, rather than left implied.

cards.title: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the states. What is one power of the states?
cards.body: There is no federal 'Department of Local Policing' -- nearly all U.S. law enforcement is organized at the state and local level.
cards.prompt: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the states. What is one power of the states?
cards.context: The 10th Amendment reserves to the states everything not explicitly given to the federal government.

cards.title: Who is the Governor of your state now?
cards.body: Some states elect governors to two-year terms, others to four -- there's no federal standard.
cards.prompt: Who is the Governor of your state now?
cards.context: Each state's chief executive is elected independently of the federal government.

cards.title: What is the capital of your state?
cards.body: Albany, Sacramento, and Springfield are all state capitals that are not their state's largest city.
cards.prompt: What is the capital of your state?
cards.context: State capitals aren't always the largest city -- politics and geography, not population, often decided the choice.

cards.title: What are the two major political parties in the United States?
cards.body: The modern Republican Party was founded in 1854; the Democratic Party traces to the 1820s, making it one of the world's oldest active parties.
cards.prompt: What are the two major political parties in the United States?
cards.context: The U.S. effectively runs a two-party system, reinforced by winner-take-all elections rather than proportional representation.

cards.title: What is the political party of the President now?
cards.body: Divided government -- a President of one party facing a Congress controlled partly or fully by the other -- has been the norm more often than not since the 1970s.
cards.prompt: What is the political party of the President now?
cards.context: This tracks whichever party the sitting President belongs to.

cards.title: What is the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives now?
cards.body: The Speaker doesn't have to be a sitting member of Congress by the Constitution's text, though in practice every Speaker has been.
cards.prompt: What is the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives now?
cards.context: The Speaker is second in the presidential line of succession, right after the Vice President.

cards.title: There are four amendments to the Constitution about who can vote. Describe one of them.
cards.body: It took over 150 years from the Constitution's ratification to reach universal adult suffrage on paper.
cards.prompt: There are four amendments to the Constitution about who can vote. Describe one of them.
cards.context: The 15th, 19th, 24th, and 26th Amendments each expanded the franchise -- by race, then sex, then removing poll taxes, then age.
answers: You don't have to pay (a poll tax) to vote.
Any citizen can vote. (Women and men can vote.)
A male citizen of any race (can vote).

cards.title: What is one responsibility that is only for United States citizens?
cards.body: Jury service is treated as both a right and a civic duty -- the 6th and 7th Amendments guarantee trial by jury.
cards.prompt: What is one responsibility that is only for United States citizens?
cards.context: Permanent residents pay taxes and can be drafted in some contexts, but jury duty and federal voting are citizen-only obligations and rights.

cards.title: Name one right only for United States citizens.
cards.body: A President must be a natural-born citizen -- the only office with that specific requirement.
cards.prompt: Name one right only for United States citizens.
cards.context: Non-citizens, even permanent residents, cannot vote in federal elections or hold federal office.

cards.title: What are two rights of everyone living in the United States?
cards.body: This is a key distinction on the test: citizen-only rights (voting) versus everyone's rights (speech, worship).
cards.prompt: What are two rights of everyone living in the United States?
cards.context: Most Bill of Rights protections apply to 'persons,' not just citizens -- they cover everyone on U.S. soil.

cards.title: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
cards.body: The Pledge was written in 1892 and only got 'under God' added by Congress in 1954.
cards.prompt: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
cards.context: The Pledge, as recited, is an oath to the flag and 'the Republic for which it stands' -- not to any individual leader.

cards.title: What is one promise you make when you become a United States citizen?
cards.body: The oath can be modified for those with religious objections to bearing arms -- they can swear to noncombatant service instead.
cards.prompt: What is one promise you make when you become a United States citizen?
cards.context: This is the Oath of Allegiance, the final legal step of naturalization.
answers: give up loyalty to other countries
defend the Constitution and laws of the United States
obey the laws of the United States
serve in the U.S. military (if needed)
serve (do important work for) the nation (if needed)
be loyal to the United States

cards.title: How old do citizens have to be to vote for President?
cards.body: 'Old enough to fight, old enough to vote' was the actual slogan of the movement behind the 26th Amendment.
cards.prompt: How old do citizens have to be to vote for President?
cards.context: The voting age was lowered from 21 to 18 by the 26th Amendment, driven largely by Vietnam-era arguments that draft-age citizens should get a vote.

cards.title: What are two ways that Americans can participate in their democracy?
cards.body: Petitioning the government -- writing, calling, showing up -- is itself a First Amendment-protected right, not just a courtesy.
cards.prompt: What are two ways that Americans can participate in their democracy?
cards.context: Voting is only one form of civic participation among many the Constitution protects.
answers: give an elected official your opinion on an issue
publicly support or oppose an issue or policy

cards.title: When is the last day you can send in federal income tax forms?
cards.body: The federal income tax itself only became permanent with the 16th Amendment in 1913.
cards.prompt: When is the last day you can send in federal income tax forms?
cards.context: This deadline is set by federal statute, not the Constitution, and can shift slightly for weekends and holidays.

cards.title: When must all men register for the Selective Service?
cards.body: Selective Service registration applies to male immigrants living in the U.S. too, including many green card holders.
cards.prompt: When must all men register for the Selective Service?
cards.context: Registration keeps a pool of eligible names on file in case a draft were ever reinstated -- there hasn't been an active draft since 1973.

cards.title: What is one reason colonists came to America?
cards.body: Many early colonists arrived as indentured servants, working years of unpaid labor to pay off the cost of the voyage.
cards.prompt: What is one reason colonists came to America?
cards.context: Motives varied hugely by colony and era -- Puritans fleeing religious conflict, debtors seeking a fresh start, merchants chasing trade.

cards.title: Who lived in America before the Europeans arrived?
cards.body: Estimates of the pre-contact Native population of North America range from several million to over 10 million.
cards.prompt: Who lived in America before the Europeans arrived?
cards.context: Hundreds of distinct nations and cultures inhabited the continent for thousands of years before European contact.

cards.title: What group of people was taken to America and sold as slaves?
cards.body: The first recorded Africans in English North America arrived at Point Comfort, Virginia, in 1619.
cards.prompt: What group of people was taken to America and sold as slaves?
cards.context: The transatlantic slave trade forcibly brought an estimated 12.5 million Africans across the Atlantic over roughly 350 years.

cards.title: Why did the colonists fight the British?
cards.body: The Quartering Act, which forced colonists to house British troops, later inspired the Third Amendment.
cards.prompt: Why did the colonists fight the British?
cards.context: Colonists paid taxes to a Parliament they had no elected representation in -- the core grievance behind 'taxation without representation.'
answers: because of high taxes (taxation without representation)
because the British army stayed in their houses (boarding, quartering)

cards.title: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?
cards.body: John Adams and Benjamin Franklin were both on that editing committee and made notable changes to Jefferson's draft.
cards.prompt: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?
cards.context: Jefferson drafted it at 33, drawing on Enlightenment political philosophy, while a five-man committee reviewed and edited his text.

cards.title: When was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
cards.body: Most delegates didn't actually sign the engrossed copy until August 2, 1776, weeks after adoption.
cards.prompt: When was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
cards.context: The Continental Congress voted for independence on July 2 but formally adopted the Declaration's text two days later.

cards.title: There were 13 original states. Name three.
cards.body: The 13 stripes on the U.S. flag represent these same 13 original states, not the current 50.
cards.prompt: There were 13 original states. Name three.
cards.context: These 13 British colonies declared independence together in 1776 and became the founding states of the Union.

cards.title: What happened at the Constitutional Convention?
cards.body: The convention was held in total secrecy, with windows nailed shut through a Philadelphia summer, to allow open debate.
cards.prompt: What happened at the Constitutional Convention?
cards.context: Delegates gathered in Philadelphia originally just to revise the weak Articles of Confederation -- they ended up scrapping it and starting over.
answers: The Founding Fathers wrote the Constitution.

cards.title: When was the Constitution written?
cards.body: It then took nearly a year longer for enough states to ratify it before it took effect in 1789.
cards.prompt: When was the Constitution written?
cards.context: It took the Philadelphia convention about four months to draft, from May to September 1787.

cards.title: The Federalist Papers supported the passage of the U.S. Constitution. Name one of the writers.
cards.body: Hamilton wrote the majority of the essays -- around 51 of the 85 -- often at a punishing writing pace.
cards.prompt: The Federalist Papers supported the passage of the U.S. Constitution. Name one of the writers.
cards.context: These 85 essays, published under the pen name 'Publius,' argued state by state for ratifying the new Constitution.

cards.title: What is one thing Benjamin Franklin is famous for?
cards.body: He's the only Founding Father to have signed all four major founding documents: the Declaration, the Treaty of Paris, the Treaty of Alliance with France, and the Constitution.
cards.prompt: What is one thing Benjamin Franklin is famous for?
cards.context: Franklin was 81 at the Constitutional Convention, decades older than most other delegates, and had already lived several careers.
answers: oldest member of the Constitutional Convention
first Postmaster General of the United States

cards.title: Who is the 'Father of Our Country'?
cards.body: He could have likely been President for life or even king -- he refused both.
cards.prompt: Who is the 'Father of Our Country'?
cards.context: Washington led the Continental Army through the Revolution and then set the precedent of a peaceful transfer of power by voluntarily stepping down.

cards.title: Who was the first President?
cards.body: He was inaugurated in New York City, then the nation's capital, not Washington D.C., which didn't exist yet.
cards.prompt: Who was the first President?
cards.context: Washington was elected unanimously by the Electoral College -- the only President in history to receive every vote.

cards.title: What territory did the United States buy from France in 1803?
cards.body: Napoleon sold it partly to fund his European wars and because he'd lost the ability to defend it after the Haitian Revolution.
cards.prompt: What territory did the United States buy from France in 1803?
cards.context: The purchase roughly doubled the size of the United States overnight for about $15 million -- a few cents an acre.

cards.title: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1800s.
cards.body: The White House was set on fire by British troops during the War of 1812.
cards.prompt: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1800s.
cards.context: The 1800s bracketed a young, expanding nation, from the War of 1812 through westward expansion to a war with Spain that made the U.S. a colonial power.

cards.title: Name the U.S. war between the North and the South.
cards.body: It began at Fort Sumter, South Carolina, in April 1861 and ended with Confederate surrender in April 1865.
cards.prompt: Name the U.S. war between the North and the South.
cards.context: It remains the deadliest war in American history, with roughly 620,000-750,000 deaths.

cards.title: Name one problem that led to the Civil War.
cards.body: Confederate declarations of secession explicitly named the preservation of slavery as a primary cause.
cards.prompt: Name one problem that led to the Civil War.
cards.context: Slavery's expansion into new territories was the central, unresolved conflict; economic and states'-rights arguments largely orbited around defending it.

cards.title: What was one important thing that Abraham Lincoln did?
cards.body: Lincoln was assassinated just five days after Confederate General Lee's surrender at Appomattox.
cards.prompt: What was one important thing that Abraham Lincoln did?
cards.context: Lincoln held the Union together through the war and moved the country toward ending slavery, though full abolition needed the 13th Amendment.
answers: led the United States during the Civil War

cards.title: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
cards.body: Full, nationwide abolition required the 13th Amendment two years later, in 1865.
cards.prompt: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
cards.context: It only applied to Confederate territory not under Union control -- it didn't free enslaved people in border states that stayed loyal to the Union.
answers: freed slaves in the Confederate states
freed slaves in most Southern states

cards.title: What did Susan B. Anthony do?
cards.body: She died in 1906, 14 years before the 19th Amendment gave women the vote nationwide in 1920.
cards.prompt: What did Susan B. Anthony do?
cards.context: She was arrested and fined for illegally voting in 1872, decades before women legally won that right.

cards.title: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1900s.
cards.body: The U.S. entered World War I in 1917 and World War II in 1941 -- both after years of staying officially neutral.
cards.prompt: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1900s.
cards.context: The 20th century saw the U.S. become a global military power across two world wars and several Cold War-era conflicts.
cards.subcategory: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information

cards.title: Who was President during World War I?
cards.body: Wilson later pushed for the League of Nations, a precursor to the UN -- but the U.S. Senate refused to join it.
cards.prompt: Who was President during World War I?
cards.context: Wilson led the U.S. into the war in 1917 after campaigning for reelection on keeping the country out of it.
cards.subcategory: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information

cards.title: Who was President during the Great Depression and World War II?
cards.body: His long tenure directly led to the 22nd Amendment, which later capped presidents at two terms.
cards.prompt: Who was President during the Great Depression and World War II?
cards.context: Roosevelt served an unprecedented four terms, launching the New Deal and leading the U.S. through most of WWII.
cards.subcategory: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information

cards.title: Who did the United States fight in World War II?
cards.body: The U.S. fought a genuine two-front war -- against Japan in the Pacific and Germany/Italy in Europe -- simultaneously.
cards.prompt: Who did the United States fight in World War II?
cards.context: These were the three main Axis powers; the U.S. entered the war formally after the attack on Pearl Harbor.
cards.subcategory: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information

cards.title: Before he was President, Eisenhower was a general. What war was he in?
cards.body: He later became President in 1953, one of very few generals to make that direct leap.
cards.prompt: Before he was President, Eisenhower was a general. What war was he in?
cards.context: Eisenhower served as Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, overseeing the D-Day invasion of Normandy.
cards.subcategory: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information

cards.title: During the Cold War, what was the main concern of the United States?
cards.body: The Cold War never involved direct U.S.-Soviet combat, but it fueled proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, and elsewhere.
cards.prompt: During the Cold War, what was the main concern of the United States?
cards.context: The decades-long standoff with the Soviet Union was defined by competing economic and political systems rather than direct military combat between the two powers.
cards.subcategory: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information

cards.title: What movement tried to end racial discrimination?
cards.body: It produced two landmark federal laws in quick succession: the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
cards.prompt: What movement tried to end racial discrimination?
cards.context: The movement used protests, litigation, and legislation to dismantle Jim Crow segregation, especially through the 1950s-60s.
cards.subcategory: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information

cards.title: What did Martin Luther King, Jr. do?
cards.body: He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 at age 35, one of the youngest laureates ever.
cards.prompt: What did Martin Luther King, Jr. do?
cards.context: King led the movement's nonviolent-resistance strategy, most famously through the 1963 March on Washington.
answers: worked for equality for all Americans

cards.title: The Tenth Amendment
cards.body: Powers not delegated to the United States, nor prohibited to the states, are reserved to the states — or to the people. Eleven words that started every states' rights argument since 1791.
cards.prompt: The Tenth Amendment

cards.title: Federalism
cards.body: One country, two full governments over every citizen: national and state. Each has its own laws, courts, and taxes. The Constitution is the referee.
cards.prompt: Federalism

cards.title: The Supremacy Clause
cards.body: When a valid federal law and a state law collide, federal law wins — Article VI calls the Constitution 'the supreme Law of the Land.'
cards.prompt: The Supremacy Clause

cards.title: Reserved Powers
cards.body: Schools, police, licenses, marriage, zoning, most criminal law — the everyday machinery of life is run by states because the Constitution never gave it to Washington.
cards.prompt: Reserved Powers

cards.title: Concurrent Powers
cards.body: Some powers are shared: taxing, borrowing, building roads, running courts. Two governments, both with their hands in your wallet, legally.
cards.prompt: Concurrent Powers

cards.title: Full Faith and Credit
cards.body: Article IV makes states honor each other's public acts, records, and court judgments — your license and your marriage travel with you across state lines.
cards.prompt: Full Faith and Credit

cards.title: State Constitutions
cards.body: Every state has its own constitution — most are longer than the federal one, and several are older. States are laboratories with their own rulebooks.
cards.prompt: State Constitutions

cards.title: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
cards.body: Maryland tried to tax the national bank. Chief Justice Marshall said no: implied federal powers are real, and 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy.'
cards.prompt: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)

cards.title: Amendment 1
cards.body: Freedom of speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition.
cards.prompt: Which amendment: Freedom of speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition.
cards.context: Five distinct freedoms in one amendment -- all aimed at keeping government out of belief, expression, and organizing.

cards.title: Amendment 2
cards.body: Right to keep and bear arms.
cards.prompt: Which amendment: Right to keep and bear arms.
cards.context: Its exact scope -- individual right versus militia context -- has been a live legal argument for over two centuries.

cards.title: Amendment 3
cards.body: No quartering of soldiers in private homes without consent.
cards.prompt: Which amendment: No quartering of soldiers in private homes without consent.
cards.context: Directly inspired by pre-Revolution Quartering Acts that forced colonists to house British troops -- the least litigated amendment in American history.

cards.title: Amendment 4
cards.body: Protection from unreasonable search and seizure.
cards.prompt: Which amendment: Protection from unreasonable search and seizure.
cards.context: Requires probable cause and, generally, a warrant -- the foundation of modern search-and-seizure law.

cards.title: Amendment 5
cards.body: Right to due process, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination.
cards.prompt: Which amendment: Right to due process, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination.
cards.context: 'Pleading the Fifth' comes directly from this amendment's protection against being forced to testify against yourself.

cards.title: Amendment 6
cards.body: Right to a speedy, public trial by an impartial jury and to legal counsel.
cards.prompt: Which amendment: Right to a speedy, public trial by an impartial jury and to legal counsel.
cards.context: The right to a lawyer wasn't fully guaranteed for poor defendants until Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), nearly two centuries after ratification.

cards.title: Amendment 7
cards.body: Right to a jury trial in civil cases.
cards.prompt: Which amendment: Right to a jury trial in civil cases.
cards.context: Applies to federal civil suits over a set dollar threshold -- one of the few Bill of Rights protections not fully applied to state courts.

cards.title: Amendment 8
cards.body: No excessive bail or fines, no cruel and unusual punishment.
cards.prompt: Which amendment: No excessive bail or fines, no cruel and unusual punishment.
cards.context: This clause underlies most modern death-penalty and prison-conditions litigation.

cards.title: Amendment 9
cards.body: Rights not listed in the Constitution are still retained by the people.
cards.prompt: Which amendment: Rights not listed in the Constitution are still retained by the people.
cards.context: A safeguard against the argument that only explicitly listed rights exist -- added because some framers worried a Bill of Rights would be read that narrowly.

cards.title: Amendment 10
cards.body: Powers not given to the federal government belong to the states or the people.
cards.prompt: Which amendment: Powers not given to the federal government belong to the states or the people.
cards.context: The core textual basis for states'-rights and federalism arguments ever since.
